case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Federal Tort Claims Act permits a damages suit against the United States Postal Service (and the United States) for the alleged loss or deprivation of a postal customer’s property caused by USPS employees, or whether the claim is barred by an FTCA exception that restores sovereign immunity.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA), primarily 28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b), 2671–2680, including the FTCA’s exceptions in 28 U.S.C. § 2680 (especially the 'postal matter'/'loss of postal matter' exception), and related background principles involving the Westfall Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2679.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government/USPS argues that even if the complaint pleads a state-law tort theory cognizable under the FTCA’s general waiver, the lawsuit is barred by an FTCA exception (centered on claims arising from the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of postal matter). In petitioners’ view, Congress preserved sovereign immunity for this category of claims to prevent routine mail-loss disputes from becoming federal tort litigation, and the Fifth Circuit erred by reading the exception too narrowly (or by allowing artful pleading to avoid it). Petitioners also frame the question as one of maintaining the FTCA’s carefully drawn limits and not expanding liability beyond what Congress expressly waived.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Konan argues that her claim falls outside the FTCA exception because the alleged conduct is not the type of ordinary 'loss/misdelivery of mail' Congress meant to immunize (and/or because the pleaded injury is a wrongful deprivation of her property by USPS personnel rather than a service-related 'transmission' failure). Respondent, supported by amici focused on government accountability, contends that the FTCA should be construed (consistent with its text and this Court’s interpretive approach in prior FTCA cases) to preserve a meaningful remedy where federal employees allegedly cause intentional or otherwise wrongful property deprivations, and that adopting the government’s broad view would turn the FTCA’s limited exceptions into a near categorical bar—functionally leaving injured parties with 'FTCA or nothing' given the narrowing of other remedies.
key_precedents: Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006)
Buchanan v. Barr, 71 F.4th 1003 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (Walker, J., concurring)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor raise the strongest concern that Dolan cautioned against reading § 2680(b) to “immunize all postal activities,” and they would treat conversion/wrongful deprivation as categorically distinct from routine transmission failures. But Dolan’s narrowing still preserved the exception’s core for harms arising “directly or consequentially” because mail “fails to arrive at all,” and—as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes—the phrase “arising out of” directs us to the causal source of the injury (missing postal matter), not the pleaded mental state or tort label. Creating an intent-based carveout from the word “loss” would be atextual and, in a sovereign-immunity setting, would invite the artful-pleading problem Justice Gorsuch flags, effectively rewriting the FTCA’s limits. A minimalist path is to hold only that where the gravamen and damages are keyed to nonreceipt/loss of postal matter, § 2680(b) bars the FTCA claim, without addressing other postal misconduct unrelated to loss or misdelivery.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Dolan cautioned against reading § 2680(b) to “immunize all postal activities” and that conversion/wrongful deprivation is categorically different from routine transmission failures—does not overcome the statute’s text as originally understood. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch explain, “any claim arising out of the loss … of … postal matter” directs us to the causal source of the injury (nonreceipt/deprivation of mail), and “arising out of” prevents plaintiffs from evading the exception through relabeling the same missing-mail harm as intentional tort. Dolan’s limiting principle is preserved by excluding unrelated premises-liability or vehicle-accident claims, not by inserting an atextual mens rea carveout into “loss,” a word that in ordinary public meaning encompasses disappearance or deprivation regardless of intent. Given the FTCA’s limited waiver and the requirement that we apply sovereign-immunity exceptions as written, policy concerns about remedial gaps cannot justify narrowing § 2680(b) beyond its ordinary meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point—that Dolan cautioned against reading § 2680(b) to “immunize all postal activities” and that alleged conversion is qualitatively different from routine transmission failure—still does not square with the statutory text barring “any claim arising out of the loss … of … postal matter.” As the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch stress, “arising out of” is causation-focused language that prevents plaintiffs from evading the exception by relabeling a missing-mail injury as conversion; the gravamen here remains nonreceipt/deprivation of postal matter. Dolan’s limitation is satisfied by excluding premises-liability or vehicle-accident claims involving postal operations, but it does not authorize an atextual intent-based carveout from “loss,” especially in a sovereign-immunity context where we apply the waiver and its exceptions as written. Justice Jackson’s remedial-gap concern is a policy argument for Congress, not a basis to narrow § 2680(b) beyond its ordinary meaning.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that “arising out of” is breadth-conferring and guards against artful pleading where the injury is nonreceipt of mail. But Dolan’s narrowing construction matters precisely because it cabins § 2680(b) to the ordinary risks of carriage—“loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” read as a coherent set—so that the exception does not become, in Justice Kagan’s words, a near-total immunity for any postal misconduct that happens to culminate in missing mail. On the pleadings, allegations of employee conversion/wrongful deprivation are qualitatively different from a transmission mishap; treating every such claim as categorically barred because mail is missing collapses Dolan’s limiting principle and unduly restricts the FTCA’s remedial role for those most vulnerable to official wrongdoing. The artful-pleading concern can be addressed by focusing on the gravamen as plausibly alleged and permitting dismissal once the record shows the claim is, in substance, a routine delivery-failure case covered by § 2680(b).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that “arising out of” is breadth-conferring and guards against artful pleading, so we should look to causal source (nonreceipt) rather than labels like conversion. But that causal framing, applied as they propose, makes § 2680(b) dispositive whenever postal matter is missing, which in practice collapses Dolan’s limiting principle and risks “immuniz[ing] all postal activities” whenever wrongdoing is intertwined with nondelivery. Textually, the triad “loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” reads most coherently as delivery-function failures inherent in carriage; treating “loss” as any intentional deprivation makes “miscarriage” and “negligent transmission” do little work and erases the contextual narrowing Dolan supplied. I therefore would not convert § 2680(b) into a missing-mail categorical bar at the pleadings stage where the gravamen is alleged employee misconduct distinct from routine transmission failure, leaving the government to test other defenses on a developed record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the hardest point: Dolan warned against reading § 2680(b) to “immunize all postal activities,” and they would treat conversion/wrongful deprivation as categorically distinct from routine delivery failures. But Dolan’s narrowing move still preserved immunity for harms arising “directly or consequentially” because mail “fails to arrive at all,” and the statute’s trigger—“any claim arising out of the loss … of … postal matter”—turns on the causal source of the injury (missing mail), not on whether the plaintiff labels the conduct negligence or conversion. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, adopting respondent’s carve-out would invite artful pleading to expand the FTCA’s limited waiver beyond the line Congress drew, which we are not free to revise in the sovereign-immunity context. Dolan’s caution is satisfied by not extending § 2680(b) to unrelated premises-liability or vehicle-accident cases, but it does not justify inserting an atextual “intentional misconduct” exception into the word “loss.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the best counterpoint by invoking Dolan’s warning against construing § 2680(b) to “immunize all postal activities,” and by characterizing conversion/wrongful deprivation as categorically different from routine transmission failures. But Dolan’s narrowing move addressed a different overbreadth problem (premises/vehicle-type injuries) while still preserving immunity for harms arising “directly or consequentially” because mail “fails to arrive at all,” which is this case’s causal source; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, “arising out of” is designed to defeat artful pleading based on tort labels. Reading an intent-based carveout into “loss” is atextual in a sovereign-immunity exception and would effectively rewrite § 2680(b) by allowing plaintiffs to relabel missing-mail claims as conversion to escape the statutory bar. The remedial-gap concern pressed by Justice Jackson is real, but under our institutional role and the FTCA’s strict limits, it cannot justify narrowing Congress’s chosen language beyond its ordinary meaning and Dolan’s core holding.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Dolan cautioned against reading § 2680(b) to “immunize all postal activities” and that conversion is qualitatively different from routine transmission failures—does not overcome the statutory text. Section 2680(b) bars “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss … of … postal matter,” and as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, “arising out of” is breadth-conferring language that directs us to the causal source of the injury (nonreceipt/deprivation of the mail) rather than the plaintiff’s chosen tort label or the alleged mens rea. Dolan’s limiting principle is preserved by confining the exception to injuries tied to missing/misdelivered/damaged mail (and not unrelated premises or vehicle accidents), but Dolan does not supply a textual basis for an intent-based carveout from “loss.” Justice Jackson’s remedial-gap concern is real, but under strict construction of sovereign-immunity waivers, we cannot narrow an exception Congress wrote in causation terms simply to ensure a damages remedy for intentional misconduct.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point seriously: “arising out of” is broad and we should not invite artful pleading in a sovereign-immunity setting. But that causal-source framing becomes effectively dispositive whenever mail is missing, and it risks doing exactly what Dolan cautioned against—functionally “immuniz[ing] all postal activities”—because any employee misconduct involving mail can be redescribed as nonreceipt. Reading “loss” in context with “miscarriage” and “negligent transmission,” I continue to see § 2680(b) as targeting the ordinary transmission failures inherent in carriage, not categorically foreclosing claims whose gravamen is alleged wrongful deprivation/conversion at the pleading stage; the government remains free to test causation and other defenses on a developed record. Justice Gorsuch’s focus on causal source usefully flags the relabeling risk, but under a pragmatic, procedure-sensitive approach, we should not collapse distinct alleged wrongs into the exception solely because the end result is missing mail.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2680(b) withdraws the FTCA’s waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter,” and that text is most naturally read to encompass claims that turn on mail not arriving, being misdelivered, or otherwise going missing in the course of postal operations. Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv. construed the exception to cover failures in the “postal obligation to deliver mail in a timely manner to the right address,” including mail that “fails to arrive at all,” and it cautioned against expanding liability in an area Congress carved out to avoid routine delivery disputes becoming federal tort litigation. Even if respondent styles the injury as a “wrongful deprivation,” the claim still “aris[es] out of” the loss or miscarriage of postal matter, and we should resolve the case on that narrow, text-and-precedent ground to preserve the FTCA’s carefully drawn limits and institutional legitimacy. The Fifth Circuit’s narrower view risks inviting artful pleading to circumvent § 2680(b) and effectively broadens the waiver beyond what Congress clearly authorized.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver applies only where Congress has spoken clearly, and § 2680(b) expressly restores sovereign immunity for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” On the text’s most natural reading, a claim that USPS employees caused a customer’s mail or postal property to be lost or deprived “aris[es] out of” the “loss” of “postal matter,” regardless of how the plaintiff styles the state-law tort theory, so the exception controls and bars suit. Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006), confirms that when a claim falls within an FTCA exception “the bar of sovereign immunity remains,” and its narrowing construction of § 2680(b) still preserves immunity for injuries tied to mail failing to arrive, arriving late, damaged, or at the wrong address—i.e., classic “loss/miscarriage” harms. Because this case is fundamentally about deprivation of postal matter in the course of postal handling, expanding liability would contradict the statute’s text and the FTCA’s limited waiver structure in §§ 1346(b) and 2680.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2680(b) restores sovereign immunity for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter,” and the ordinary meaning of “loss” comfortably includes deprivation of mail by postal employees, whether negligent or intentional, so long as the injury stems from mail not being delivered as it should. Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv. confirms that the exception targets core delivery failures—mail that “fails to arrive at all” or is not delivered “to the right address”—and warns against expanding the FTCA beyond Congress’s carefully drawn waiver; respondent’s theory is, at bottom, a nondelivery/loss claim dressed in different tort language. Reading the exception narrowly would invite artful pleading and expose USPS to routine mail-dispute litigation that Congress meant to preclude, a practical consequence inconsistent with the FTCA’s structure and this Court’s insistence that waivers of sovereign immunity be strictly construed. Given the statutory text and Dolan’s understanding of the exception’s domain, the Fifth Circuit erred in allowing this claim to proceed notwithstanding § 2680(b).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2680(b) restores immunity only for claims “arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter,” and Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv. construes that exception narrowly—generally covering injuries traceable to mail failing to arrive, arriving late, damaged, or misdelivered, not “all postal activities.” On the pleadings described here, Konan alleges a wrongful deprivation of property by USPS personnel rather than an ordinary service-related transmission failure, and reading § 2680(b) to bar such claims would expand the exception beyond its text and Dolan’s limiting principles. Given the FTCA’s role as the primary remedial pathway against federal employees after the narrowing of alternative remedies, a broad construction would leave injured parties—often with limited resources—without a meaningful damages remedy for wrongful conduct. Accordingly, the better reading is that the FTCA waiver in 28 U.S.C. § 1346(b) applies and the § 2680(b) postal-matter exception does not.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2680(b) withdraws the FTCA’s waiver only for claims “arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter,” and in Dolan v. USPS the Court construed that exception not to “immunize all postal activities,” but generally to cover injuries that occur because mail fails to arrive, arrives late, damaged, or at the wrong address. Read textually and with Dolan’s workability guidance, a claim alleging USPS employees’ wrongful deprivation or conversion of a customer’s property is best understood as misconduct distinct from the routine risks of “loss” or “negligent transmission” inherent in mail delivery, and therefore outside § 2680(b). That narrower reading preserves statutory coherence by allowing the FTCA’s general waiver in § 1346(b) to do its intended work while keeping § 2680(b) focused on ordinary mail-carriage failures rather than creating a near-categorical immunity for any employee wrongdoing that results in missing mail.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver yields where Congress preserved immunity for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” 28 U.S.C. § 2680(b). Under Dolan v. USPS, that exception reaches injuries “arising, directly or consequentially, because mail either fails to arrive at all or arrives late, in damaged condition, or at the wrong address,” 546 U.S. 481, 489 (2006), and respondent’s theory—however styled as wrongful deprivation—still seeks damages because her mail did not arrive. The statutory phrase “arising out of” is broad and focuses on the causal source of the injury, so artful pleading cannot evade the exception’s plain scope; if the claim falls within § 2680(b), sovereign immunity remains. Respecting Congress’s carefully drawn limits on the waiver, the suit is barred and must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity is limited by § 2680(b), which preserves immunity for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” Under Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., that exception covers injuries arising “directly or consequentially” because mail “fails to arrive at all,” including circumstances involving non-delivery as part of postal operations. Respondent’s theory—however characterized as wrongful deprivation—still seeks damages flowing from the non-receipt of mail and therefore “aris[es] out of” the loss or miscarriage of postal matter, and courts should not allow artful pleading to expand the FTCA beyond Congress’s carefully drawn exceptions. Given the FTCA’s history and the principle that exceptions restore the “bar of sovereign immunity” when applicable, judicial restraint counsels applying § 2680(b) as written rather than creating a new carve-out for intentional non-delivery.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver does not apply to “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” 28 U.S.C. § 2680(b). Read in light of its ordinary public meaning, “loss” of postal matter encompasses a customer’s mail being deprived or not delivered as expected, regardless of whether the precipitating conduct is characterized as negligent or otherwise; allowing artful pleading to relabel a nondelivery as conversion would undercut the exception’s function of restoring sovereign immunity for mail-delivery disputes. Dolan v. USPS confirms the exception targets injuries arising “because mail either fails to arrive at all or arrives late, in damaged condition, or at the wrong address,” 546 U.S. 481, 489 (2006), and that description fits a claim premised on a customer’s property not reaching her. Because § 2680(b) applies, sovereign immunity remains and the suit is barred notwithstanding the FTCA’s general waiver in §§ 1346(b) and 2674.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2680(b) restores immunity only for claims “arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter,” and Dolan v. U.S. Postal Serv., 546 U.S. 481 (2006), construed that exception not to “immunize all postal activities” but generally to cover injuries tied to mail failing to arrive, arriving late, damaged, or at the wrong address. Taking the allegations as pleaded, the asserted harm is a wrongful deprivation of property by USPS personnel rather than a service-related “transmission” failure, and reading § 2680(b) to bar such claims would expand the exception beyond its text and Dolan’s limiting principle. Given the FTCA’s role as the primary remedial scheme for tortious “wrongful act[s] or omission[s]” of federal employees, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b), 2674, a broad construction here would have serious practical consequences by leaving individuals without a meaningful damages remedy for alleged misconduct. Accordingly, I would hold the claim not categorically barred by § 2680(b) at this stage and affirm allowing it to proceed under the FTCA’s general waiver.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Federal Tort Claims Act permits a damages suit against the United States Postal Service for postal employees’ alleged intentional misconduct (including discrimination and property deprivation), or whether an FTCA exception bars the claim and thus eliminates any tort remedy.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA), 28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b), 2671–2680 (with emphasis on the FTCA’s exceptions in 28 U.S.C. § 2680) and the Westfall Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b)(1)–(2).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government argues that respondent’s claim is barred by an FTCA exception in 28 U.S.C. § 2680, properly read to foreclose liability for the kind of conduct alleged in the handling of mail/postal operations, and that the Fifth Circuit erred by interpreting the statute too narrowly; in the government’s view, allowing the suit would expand FTCA liability beyond what Congress consented to in waiving sovereign immunity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (supported by amici) argues that the FTCA should be interpreted—consistent with its text, structure, and remedial purpose—to allow suits for intentional, wrongful acts by federal employees that would be tortious under state law, and that the government’s reading of the FTCA exceptions is overbroad and would effectively make the FTCA a dead letter in many real-world accountability cases (especially given the contraction of Bivens remedies); respondent urges affirmance of the Fifth Circuit’s more limited view of the exception so that victims are not left with 'FTCA or nothing' turning into 'nothing.'
key_precedents: Dolan v. U.S. Postal Service, 546 U.S. 481 (2006)
Buchanan v. Barr, 71 F.4th 1003 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (Walker, J., concurring)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s remedial-gap concern is the strongest counterweight here, particularly in light of Abbasi and Egbert, but under our sovereign-immunity cases the FTCA’s waiver in § 1346(b) is expressly “subject to” the exceptions in § 2680, so we cannot narrow § 2680(b) to avoid policy consequences. As Justice Kagan stresses, the gravamen of this complaint is nondelivery/withholding of mail; Dolan’s narrowing was aimed at excluding distinct premises-liability-type injuries, while reaffirming that claims for harms arising “directly or consequentially” from mail that fails to arrive fall within the postal exception. Justice Thomas’s ordinary-meaning point about “miscarriage” reinforces that the operative question is whether the injury arises out of delivery failure, not the actor’s intent, and an intent-based carveout would effectively expand the waiver beyond the statutory boundary. A minimalist opinion can hold only that where the alleged injury is rooted in the loss/miscarriage of postal matter—however pleaded—§ 2680(b) bars the FTCA claim, leaving any broader remedial adjustments to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s remedial-gap argument, sharpened by her reading of Dolan as a narrowing decision, is the best case for respondent, but it cannot overcome the enacted text in a sovereign-immunity exception. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1346(b)’s waiver is expressly “subject to” § 2680, and Dolan’s narrowing concerned excluding premises-liability-type injuries—not creating an intent-based carveout where the injury still flows from mail that “fails to arrive at all.” On the ordinary public meaning, “miscarriage” encompasses a failure in proper carriage or delivery, and a claim alleging intentional withholding still “aris[es] out of” that miscarriage because the harm is nondelivery itself. Any resulting remedial shortfall after Abbasi/Egbert is a policy matter for Congress, not a license for us to rewrite § 2680(b).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s remedial-gap point is the hardest: after Abbasi and Egbert, a broad reading of § 2680(b) may leave intentional, discriminatory withholding of mail without a damages remedy. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, the FTCA’s waiver is expressly “subject to” § 2680, and § 2680(b)’s text bars “any claim arising out of the loss [or] miscarriage” of mail—language that turns on the nature of the injury (nondelivery/failure in carriage), not the actor’s motive. Dolan’s narrowing, as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett note, was aimed at excluding premises-liability-type injuries from “negligent transmission,” not creating an intent-based carveout for nondelivery itself; extending Dolan to exempt intentional nondelivery would rewrite the exception beyond its ordinary meaning. Whatever the practical consequences, sovereign-immunity rules require a clear congressional statement to expand liability, and the Westfall Act channeling only underscores that any remedial adjustment must come from Congress, not us.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to emphasize that § 1346(b)’s waiver is “subject to” § 2680 and that we cannot manufacture a remedy simply because Abbasi/Egbert have narrowed other avenues; sovereign-immunity limits must be taken seriously. But their gravamen framing proves too much here: treating any intentional, discriminatory withholding as a claim “arising out of” a “miscarriage” collapses Dolan’s context-sensitive narrowing into near-total immunity whenever misconduct is executed through the mail, contrary to Dolan’s warning against reading § 2680’s categorical exceptions to swallow the FTCA’s remedial core. Justice Thomas’s ordinary-meaning account of “miscarriage” also ignores the statutory pairing—“loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission”—which signals routine operational failures in carriage, not purposeful deprivation that functions as a distinct wrong. Given the Westfall Act channeling Roberts and Kagan stress, a broad construction predictably creates a remedial dead zone for vulnerable plaintiffs, and in a close textual context Dolan supports holding the postal exception to its core: ordinary delivery failures, not intentional abuse of postal processes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Dolan cautioned against reading § 2680(b) so broadly that it becomes sweeping immunity for any misconduct touching the mail, and the remedial-gap concern is heightened post-Abbasi/Egbert. But Dolan’s narrowing was about excluding distinct, non-mail-harm torts (like premises-type injuries) from “negligent transmission,” while still confirming that harms flowing “directly or consequentially” from mail that fails to arrive fall within the exception—here, the gravamen is nondelivery/withholding itself, even if relabeled as intentional discrimination. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 1346(b)’s waiver is expressly “subject to” § 2680, and under the Westfall Act channeling we cannot preserve FTCA jurisdiction by recharacterizing the same delivery-failure injury as a different tort label without effectively adding an intent-based carveout Congress did not write. The policy discomfort is real, but under a pragmatic textualist approach the workable, coherent line is to apply § 2680(b) to claims whose injury depends on loss/miscarriage/nondelivery of mail and leave any remedial expansion to Congress.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: Dolan cautioned against reading § 2680(b) so broadly that it becomes a sweeping immunity for any postal-related misconduct, especially given today’s limited Bivens landscape. But under the text Congress enacted, the dispositive question is whether the claim “aris[es] out of” the “loss” or “miscarriage” of postal matter, and (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize) the gravamen here is nondelivery itself—an injury Dolan described as covered “directly or consequentially” when mail fails to arrive. Dolan’s narrowing addressed different harms (like slip-and-fall premises liability) and does not supply an intent-based carveout; importing motive limits into a sovereign-immunity exception would expand the FTCA waiver beyond what Congress “clearly said.” The remedial-gap concern is real, but as Justice Thomas notes, it cannot justify rewriting § 2680(b)’s boundary, particularly where the Westfall Act channels employee torts into the FTCA and leaves any adjustment to Congress.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s remedial-gap argument remains the most serious counterpoint—especially given Abbasi and Egbert—but under sovereign-immunity principles we cannot narrow § 2680(b) based on the desirability of a damages remedy. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the waiver in § 1346(b) is expressly “subject to” § 2680, and Dolan’s context-sensitive narrowing addressed slip-and-fall/premises injuries, not an intent-based carveout where the gravamen is nondelivery itself. On the text, I agree with Justice Thomas that a claim premised on intentional withholding still “aris[es] out of” the “loss” or “miscarriage” of postal matter because the injury flows from the failure of carriage/delivery, regardless of motive. Any resulting remedial deficiency given the Westfall Act’s channeling is for Congress to correct, not for us to revise the exception’s ordinary meaning.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Dolan cautioned against reading § 2680(b) so broadly that it becomes sweeping immunity for postal misconduct, especially given the contraction of Bivens. But Dolan’s narrowing was targeted to separate mail-delivery failures (covered) from distinct premises-liability injuries (not covered), and it reaffirmed that § 2680(b) reaches harms arising “directly or consequentially” from mail that fails to arrive—precisely the gravamen here even if the nondelivery is alleged to be intentional. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, § 1346(b)’s waiver is expressly “subject to” § 2680, and the Westfall Act’s channeling makes it improper to preserve FTCA jurisdiction by relabeling a nondelivery claim as discrimination or another tort while the injury still “aris[es] out of” loss/miscarriage of mail. The remedial-gap concern is serious, but under sovereign-immunity principles we cannot create an intent-based carveout that Congress did not textually provide.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the most textually grounded point: § 1346(b)’s waiver is expressly “subject to” § 2680, and Dolan did say the exception covers harms flowing “directly or consequentially” from mail that fails to arrive. But I do not read Dolan as licensing an unlimited “gravamen = nondelivery” rule that would immunize distinct, purposeful abuse of postal processes simply because the mechanism involves mail; Dolan’s context-sensitive narrowing was aimed at keeping § 2680(b) tethered to core, routine mail-delivery failures rather than becoming a catchall shield. Justice Barrett’s concern about an atextual intent-based carveout is serious, yet under my pragmatic, procedure-focused approach the limiting principle can come from the statute’s structure—“loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” read in context—without rewriting it to turn every intentional deprivation into a barred “miscarriage.” Given the remedial realities after Abbasi/Egbert (a point even Roberts acknowledges as serious), I would not extend § 2680(b) to foreclose these claims absent clearer congressional direction that intentional, targeted interference is treated the same as ordinary delivery mishaps.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity in 28 U.S.C. § 1346(b) is expressly “subject to” the exceptions in § 2680, and we have repeatedly treated those exceptions as limits Congress set on the scope of consent to suit. Although Dolan v. U.S. Postal Service, 546 U.S. 481 (2006), construed § 2680(b)’s “postal matter” exception narrowly in context, it still reaffirmed that claims “arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of mail are barred—precisely the sort of boundary-setting that preserves the statute’s coherent scheme and the Government’s immunity where Congress has not clearly waived it. Given the Westfall Act’s channeling of employee tort suits into the FTCA, 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b)(1), it is for Congress—not this Court—to expand remedies when an exception applies, particularly in light of our reluctance to create alternative damages actions outside statutory authorization (Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S. 482 (2022)). A narrow holding recognizing the exception’s applicability here best respects precedent, avoids enlarging the waiver beyond its text, and protects institutional legitimacy by leaving any remedial gap to the legislative branch.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity applies only within the bounds Congress set, and § 2680(b) expressly withholds that waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” Under the ordinary public meaning of “miscarriage” as a failure in proper carriage or delivery, respondent’s allegations that postal employees intentionally failed to deliver her mail still “aris[e] out of” a miscarriage of mail, so the exception applies and sovereign immunity remains. Dolan v. U.S. Postal Service confirms that § 2680(b) retains immunity for injuries arising directly or consequentially from mail failing to arrive or arriving improperly, and this case fits that description. Because the exception removes the FTCA cause of action regardless of the absence of alternative remedies, the Fifth Circuit’s narrower reading improperly expands the waiver beyond the text Congress enacted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity must be read narrowly, and § 2680(b) expressly preserves immunity for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter,” which by its text is not limited to negligent mishandling. As Dolan v. U.S. Postal Service construed the exception to cover injuries arising “directly or consequentially” from mail that fails to arrive, arrives late, damaged, or at the wrong address, respondent’s alleged harms rooted in nondelivery/withholding of mail fall within the exception even if the conduct is alleged to be intentional. The practical consequence of respondent’s reading would expand FTCA liability beyond the limited consent Congress granted, contrary to the structure of § 2680’s categorical carveouts. Whatever remedial gaps exist after this Court’s Bivens decisions (e.g., Egbert v. Boule) do not justify rewriting § 2680(b) to create tort remedies Congress withheld.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FTCA’s postal-matter exception, 28 U.S.C. § 2680(b), should be read narrowly, consistent with Dolan v. U.S. Postal Service, which limited the exception to harms stemming from ordinary failures of delivery—mail arriving late, damaged, misdelivered, or not arriving—rather than insulating intentional, discriminatory misconduct that deprives individuals of property and access to essential communications. Given the Court’s contraction of implied constitutional remedies (Egbert v. Boule; Ziglar v. Abbasi), an overbroad construction of § 2680(b) would predictably leave victims—especially vulnerable populations—without any meaningful damages remedy, contrary to the FTCA’s remedial purpose and Congress’s limited, specific drafting of the exception. The government’s reading would effectively turn a targeted exception into a sweeping immunity for wrongful conduct “arising out of” any mail-handling, a breadth Dolan cautioned against when it emphasized the exception’s specificity relative to neighboring § 2680 provisions. Because respondent plausibly alleges intentional misconduct beyond mere “negligent transmission,” the claim should proceed under § 1346(b) rather than be dismissed at the threshold.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2680(b) withdraws the FTCA’s waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of mail, and under Dolan v. U.S. Postal Service the exception generally covers injuries arising “directly or consequentially” because mail fails to arrive, arrives late, damaged, or misdelivered. Here, even if framed as intentional discrimination or property deprivation, the gravamen is non-delivery/misdelivery of postal matter and the resulting harms, so the claim still “aris[es] out of” mail loss/miscarriage within § 2680(b). The Westfall Act’s substitution rule, 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b)(1), makes the FTCA the exclusive route for covered employee torts; when an FTCA exception applies, sovereign immunity remains and there is no tort remedy in federal court. While that outcome is hard given the narrowing of Bivens (Egbert; Abbasi), Dolan’s textual construction of § 2680(b) and Congress’s retained immunity for core mail-delivery failures point to reversal.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FTCA waives sovereign immunity only to the extent Congress clearly said so, and § 2680(b) expressly withholds that waiver for “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.” Under Dolan v. U.S. Postal Service, the exception covers injuries arising “directly or consequentially” because mail “fails to arrive at all,” and respondent’s theory—intentional refusal to deliver resulting in non-receipt and related harms—still arises out of that very failure of delivery. While respondent stresses remedial purpose and the narrowing of Bivens remedies (see Ziglar and Egbert), those policy considerations cannot expand a waiver of sovereign immunity beyond the statute’s text, and the Westfall Act channels employee-tort claims into the FTCA only “subject to” its exceptions, leaving immunity intact where § 2680 applies. Because § 2680(b) applies on its terms as construed in Dolan, the claim is barred and no tort remedy lies absent further congressional authorization.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity is limited by its exceptions, and § 2680(b) bars “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter,” which is best read—consistent with the statute’s text—to cover claims predicated on the non-delivery/deprivation of mail even when the alleged misconduct is intentional. While Dolan v. U.S. Postal Service construed the postal-matter exception narrowly, it emphasized fidelity to the exception’s text and Congress’s choices, and here the claim still “arises out of” loss/miscarriage of postal matter within § 2680(b). Given the Court’s modern reluctance to create alternative damages remedies where Congress has not authorized them (Egbert v. Boule; Ziglar v. Abbasi), it is not the judiciary’s role to narrow a sovereign-immunity exception to avoid remedial gaps. Practical workability and institutional legitimacy also favor adhering to the FTCA’s clear limits rather than expanding liability beyond what Congress consented to in § 2680.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FTCA’s waiver of sovereign immunity is limited by § 2680(b), which bars “[a]ny claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter,” and that text contains no limitation to merely negligent “loss” or “miscarriage.” Under Dolan v. U.S. Postal Service, § 2680(b) covers injuries arising “directly or consequentially” because mail “fails to arrive at all” or is delivered late, damaged, or to the wrong address, and respondent’s theory—intentional refusal to deliver—still “arises out of” nondelivery. Given the canon that waivers of sovereign immunity must be strictly construed and the Westfall Act’s channeling of employee torts into the FTCA, the statutory scheme indicates Congress preserved immunity for this class of mail-handling claims even if it leaves some plaintiffs without a tort remedy. The Fifth Circuit’s narrower construction would effectively add an intent-based carveout not found in the statute’s original public meaning and would expand liability beyond what Congress consented to.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2680(b) withdraws the FTCA waiver for “loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission” of mail, and Dolan v. U.S. Postal Service construed that exception in a practical, context-sensitive way—aimed at routine delivery failures, not as a blanket immunity for intentional, discriminatory abuse of postal processes. Reading “miscarriage” and “loss” to categorically encompass purposeful misconduct would be an overbroad construction that risks making the FTCA’s remedial scheme illusory in real-world accountability cases, especially given the Court’s contraction of Bivens remedies in Ziglar v. Abbasi and Egbert v. Boule. Consistent with procedural fairness and the FTCA’s design to provide state-law tort remedies where the Government has consented, I would not extend § 2680(b) beyond the core mail-delivery harms Dolan identified, absent clearer congressional direction. Accordingly, I would affirm the Fifth Circuit’s narrower view so that a tort remedy is not eliminated by an expansive exception.
